edges.basis: The sources independently preserve the relationship named by delivered to gentiles / delivered to gentiles. The two predictions align in movement while selecting different verbs and time phrasing.
edges.label: Delivered to Gentiles / delivered to Gentiles

edges.basis: The sources independently preserve the relationship named by handwashing / pleasing the multitude. The verdict is shared while each witness supplies a distinct account of Pilate and the crowd.
edges.label: Handwashing / pleasing the multitude

edges.basis: The sources independently preserve the relationship named by no capital charge / no basis for a charge. Repeated declarations of no guilt stand beside a verdict produced under sustained pressure.
edges.label: No capital charge / no basis for a charge

edges.basis: The sources independently preserve the relationship named by compelled to carry / carries behind jesus. The shared carrier enters two differently populated and spoken scenes.
edges.label: Compelled to carry / carries behind Jesus

edges.basis: The sources independently preserve the relationship named by the third hour / about the sixth hour. The explicit time statements occur at different narrative moments and resist casual alignment.
edges.label: The third hour / about the sixth hour

edges.basis: The sources independently preserve the relationship named by both reproach / one rebukes the other. The witnesses describe the speech of those crucified beside Jesus differently.
edges.label: Both reproach / one rebukes the other

edges.basis: The sources independently preserve the relationship named by opened tombs / witnesses at a distance. A shared darkness, cry, death, and torn veil are surrounded by differently selected signs and witnesses.
edges.label: Opened tombs / witnesses at a distance

edges.basis: The sources independently preserve the relationship named by son of god / certainly a righteous man. The same witness role is preserved with different reported words and surrounding responses.
edges.label: Son of God / certainly a righteous man

edges.basis: The sources independently preserve the relationship named by why have you forsaken me? / into your hands. The witnesses preserve different final speech without supplying a combined sequence.
edges.label: Why have you forsaken me? / into your hands

edges.basis: The sources independently preserve the relationship named by king of the jews / jesus the nazarene, king of the jews. The royal charge is shared while John expands its wording, readership, and dispute.
edges.label: King of the Jews / Jesus the Nazarene, King of the Jews

edges.basis: The sources independently preserve the relationship named by garments divided / scripture fulfilled. Shared garment language moves from a psalmic speaker into an explicitly cited narrated action.
edges.label: Garments divided / Scripture fulfilled

edges.basis: The sources independently preserve the relationship named by look on the pierced one / they will look on him whom they pierced. John cites the prophetic wording inside a specific witnessed sequence without reproducing Zechariah’s whole mourning scene.
edges.label: Look on the pierced one / they will look on him whom they pierced

edges.basis: The sources independently preserve the relationship named by joseph alone named / joseph and nicodemus. The burial is shared while confirmation, witnesses, helpers, materials, and location are selected differently.
edges.label: Joseph alone named / Joseph and Nicodemus

edges.basis: The sources independently preserve the relationship named by pentecost speech / council defense. The same crucified-and-raised identification serves two different public situations.
edges.label: Pentecost speech / council defense

edges.basis: The sources independently preserve the relationship named by message of the cross / obedience to cross-death. The cross is central in both passages while doing distinct work in two different arguments.
edges.label: Message of the cross / obedience to cross-death

edges.basis: The sources independently preserve the relationship named by hostility ended / peace made. Both passages use cross-language for reconciliation while naming different scopes and surrounding images.
edges.label: Hostility ended / peace made

edges.basis: The sources independently preserve the relationship named by wounded servant / wounds remembered. The later passage gathers servant-language around Christ while addressing a different audience and immediate concern.
edges.label: Wounded servant / wounds remembered

edges.basis: The sources independently preserve the relationship named by the disciples grieve / the disciples fear to ask. The prediction is closely aligned while each witness selects a different response from the disciples.
edges.label: The disciples grieve / the disciples fear to ask

edges.basis: The sources independently preserve the relationship named by simon is compelled / jesus bears the cross. The witnesses identify the bearer on the journey differently without explaining how their selected details relate.
edges.label: Simon is compelled / Jesus bears the cross

edges.basis: The sources independently preserve the relationship named by covenant blood at the table / the lord’s death proclaimed. The meal scene and the received communal tradition share actions and elements while speaking from different moments.
edges.label: Covenant blood at the table / the Lord’s death proclaimed

edges.basis: The sources independently preserve the relationship named by prophets announced suffering / the servant bears and is wounded. Peter makes a broad prophetic claim while Isaiah’s source preserves its own extended speaker, servant, and sequence.
edges.label: Prophets announced suffering / the servant bears and is wounded

edges.basis: The sources independently preserve the relationship named by enemies reconciled / one died for all. Both passages connect death and reconciliation while arranging the actors, scope, and consequences differently.

edges.basis: The sources independently preserve the relationship named by received tradition / synagogue proclamation. The event sequence is stable while received tradition and public address select different witnesses and explanatory details.
edges.label: Received tradition / synagogue proclamation

edges.basis: Matthew first narrates resistance to the suffering announcement, then preserves a later prediction with a more detailed custody sequence. The first scene foregrounds Peter’s resistance and discipleship speech; the road scene foregrounds actors, treatment, and third-day timing.
edges.label: First disclosure / road detail

edges.basis: Luke and Mark preserve closely placed road predictions while Luke explicitly names prophetic writing and lack of understanding. One witness emphasizes what remains hidden from the Twelve; the other expands the sequence of human actions.
edges.label: Prophetic frame / narrated sequence

edges.basis: John uses lifted-up language in two distinct settings and later explains that it signals the kind of death Jesus would die. The earlier passage compares the Son of Man with Moses’ serpent; the later passage adds hour, voice, judgment, attraction, and narrated explanation.
edges.label: Serpent lifted / death signaled

edges.basis: Jesus’ road prediction can be inspected beside the later Passover announcement and leaders’ plot. The prediction names a future custody chain; the later scene places Jesus’ announcement beside a plan shaped by feast timing.
edges.label: Approach named / leaders gather

edges.basis: Matthew and Mark independently preserve the soldiers’ mock kingship sequence. Both name thorns, salute, blows, and removal of the costume while differing in clothing description and selected gestures.
edges.label: Scarlet robe / purple robe

edges.basis: John’s first Pilate exchange and Matthew’s sentencing sequence independently preserve kingship, accusation, Barabbas, and a release choice. John concentrates on kingship, truth, and the accusers’ position; Matthew adds warning, handwashing, crowd response, flogging, and delivery.
edges.label: Kingship and truth / release and delivery

edges.basis: Matthew and Luke preserve distinct closures to the burial sequence. Matthew continues to sealing and a guard on the next day; Luke closes with women preparing spices and resting according to the commandment.
edges.label: Guarded tomb / Sabbath rest

edges.basis: Luke places an uncertain traveler retelling beside a later public speech that orders death, raising, witness, exaltation, and Spirit. The travelers possess reports without recognition; Peter addresses a public audience with a concluded proclamation.
edges.label: Unresolved retelling / public proclamation

edges.basis: Peter’s council answer and household speech both name death on a tree, divine action, and witness in different settings. The council scene emphasizes obedience under prohibition; the household speech emphasizes public deeds, chosen witnesses, and commanded proclamation.
edges.label: Council witness / household witness

edges.basis: Paul uses participation in Christ’s death within two different arguments about continuing life. Romans organizes the claim through baptism, burial, slavery, and new life; Galatians organizes it through law, faith, self, and the Son’s self-giving.
edges.label: Death in baptism / crucified with Christ

edges.basis: Two Pauline arguments recall how the crucified Christ was first presented to their hearers. Corinthians contrasts proclamations and wisdoms; Galatians challenges a changed response after a prior public portrayal.
edges.label: Crucified proclamation / public portrayal

edges.basis: Both passages take up execution-tree language while making different claims about curse, bearing, wounds, and resulting life. Galatians works through law, curse, Abrahamic blessing, and Spirit; 1 Peter addresses suffering conduct, non-retaliation, wounds, and return.
edges.label: Curse language / sins borne

edges.basis: The cross appears as the exclusive ground of boasting in one passage and as endured shame in another. Galatians contrasts circumcision, persecution, world, and new creation; Hebrews places cross and shame inside an appeal to run with endurance.
edges.label: Boasting in the cross / enduring the cross

edges.basis: The two passages describe different obstacles removed in relation to the cross. Colossians names trespasses, a written record, rulers, and triumph; Ephesians names divided peoples, law, hostility, one body, and access.
edges.label: Record removed / hostility killed

edges.basis: John’s repeated lifted-up sayings can be read in their distinct disputes and narrative explanations. The first links lifting up with recognition and divine speech; the later links it with hour, judgment, attraction, and the kind of death.
edges.label: Then you will know / kind of death

edges.basis: Luke and Matthew preserve distinct meal sequences immediately before the arrest. Luke names desire, remembrance, kingdom, and a betraying hand; Matthew names covenant blood, forgiveness, future drinking, and departure.
edges.label: Desired Passover / covenant cup

edges.basis: The shepherd’s voluntary laying down of life is later used as the stated way love becomes known. John’s Gospel emphasizes authority, sheep, taking up life, and the Father’s command; the letter turns the laid-down life toward material care for others.
edges.label: Shepherd lays down life / love known

edges.basis: A council’s decision that one man should die can be inspected beside Paul’s later account of rulers, condemnation, tree, tomb, raising, and forgiveness. John attributes an unintended wider statement to the high priest; Acts presents a retrospective proclamation to a synagogue audience.
edges.label: One should die / death publicly recounted

edges.basis: Matthew and John preserve distinct actions immediately before and during the arrest. Matthew foregrounds repeated prayer, sleeping disciples, betrayal, flight, and Scripture; John foregrounds Jesus’ self-identification, the party falling back, protection of disciples, and the cup.
edges.label: Prayer before arrest / stepping forward

edges.basis: Matthew’s council hearing and John’s inside-outside sequence preserve different testimony and denial structures. Matthew moves through failed witnesses to the high priest’s question and condemnation; John alternates Jesus’ questioning with Peter’s denials.
edges.label: Council testimony / questioning and denial

edges.basis: Acts explicitly begins good news about Jesus from a bounded reading of Isaiah’s silent-sheep language. Isaiah preserves an extended servant poem; Acts preserves a reader’s question and an apostolic interpretation without reproducing the whole source.
edges.label: Silent sheep read / servant passage heard

edges.basis: Paul’s synagogue reasoning that the Christ had to suffer can be held beside Jesus’ first explicit disclosure and Peter’s resistance. Acts summarizes a repeated scriptural argument; Matthew narrates one disclosure, rebuke, and call to discipleship.
edges.label: Scriptural reasoning / first disclosure

edges.basis: Romans develops the significance of Christ’s death through distinct arguments about righteousness and reconciliation. The first passage centers manifested righteousness, redemption, blood, and God’s justice; the second centers weakness, enemies, death, blood, rescue, and rejoicing.
edges.label: Redemption displayed / enemies reconciled

edges.basis: Hebrews’ prepared-body argument can be inspected beside its sanctuary and own-blood argument. Chapter 9 works through sanctuary, covenant, blood, death, and entry; chapter 10 works through repeated offerings, a prepared body, obedience, sitting down, and remembered sins.
edges.label: Prepared body / own blood

edges.basis: Both passages connect Jesus’ suffering with a place or object of reproach while addressing hearers’ response. Hebrews uses camp, gate, altar, blood, and bearing reproach; 1 Peter uses tree, wounds, non-retaliation, and return to the shepherd.
edges.label: Outside the gate / on the tree

edges.basis: The passages independently state Christ’s death for others and name different outcomes. Peter moves through righteous and unrighteous, bringing to God, death and life, spirits, baptism, resurrection, and authority; Romans moves through weakness, enemies, blood, rescue, and reconciliation.
edges.label: Once for sins / death for enemies

edges.basis: Revelation names blood and death-memory in both an opening greeting and a throne vision. The opening names faithful witness, firstborn, ruler, love, release, and coming; the vision presents a standing slain Lamb, scroll, worship, purchased peoples, and kingdom.
edges.label: Witness who freed / Lamb who purchased

event.centerRule: Jesus remains the central person of the Event. Each Gospel witness, later proclamation, and letter reuse remains attached to its own canonical source rather than being merged into a synthetic harmony.

characterAnchors.label: Jesus
characterAnchors.note: Predicts what approaches, is sentenced and crucified, speaks from the cross, dies, is buried, and is named in later proclamation and memory.

characterAnchors.note: Questions Jesus, responds to accusers and crowds, authorizes the sentence, and later answers burial requests.

characterAnchors.label: Chief priests and elders
characterAnchors.note: Accuse, press claims, answer Pilate, mock, and act around the tomb in selected witnesses.

characterAnchors.label: Soldiers
characterAnchors.note: Mock, lead, crucify, divide garments, guard, inspect bodies, and respond within the Gospel accounts.

characterAnchors.label: Simon of Cyrene
characterAnchors.note: Is compelled to carry the cross in the Synoptic witnesses.

characterAnchors.label: Women witnesses
characterAnchors.note: Follow, mourn, watch from a distance, observe burial, prepare spices, and later hear the Crucifixion recalled.

characterAnchors.label: Joseph of Arimathea
characterAnchors.note: Requests Jesus’ body and acts in all four burial witnesses.

characterAnchors.label: Nicodemus
characterAnchors.note: Joins Joseph with spices and linen in John’s burial account.

characterAnchors.label: Apostolic witnesses
characterAnchors.note: Name the Event before different audiences in Acts and later writing.

event.throughline: Jesus names the approaching death; authorities, Pilate, soldiers, crowds, companions, criminals, and witnesses enter four Gospel sequences of sentencing, crucifixion, death, and burial; Acts and the letters later name and reuse the Event in distinct settings.

topic.orientation: Enter the Crucifixion through four distinct Gospel witnesses, then inspect how the Event is named in proclamation and later canonical memory. Prediction, execution, death, burial, and reuse remain connected without absorbing the separate Resurrection Event.
